Introduction

I’ve written up some wild trades before. A crypto Closed End Fund trading with 100% upside to Net Asset Value, a Jordanian Insurer at 4x Earnings, a Georgian Financial Conglomerate with 70% upside to Net Asset Value repurchasing 15% of shares a year, and a Japanese Publisher with a concealed securities portfolio repurchasing 15% of the float every year.

I don’t seek out these setups just because they are crazy or niche, rather, I’ve learned some of the best risk-to-reward setups lie in names that are off limits to larger Institutional Investors.

As a Retail Investor you have two distinct edges, no investment mandate and a significant execution advantage. Unlike Institutional Investors who have risk, liquidity, and portfolio constraints, as a Retail Investor you can trade whatever you want, whenever you want. One day you can be an AI Expert and the next day you can specialize in Women’s Jeans. I’m not saying this is the best approach to take, but the freedom to trade anything is an advantage as it allows you to pursue the most favorable risk-to-reward setups.

Secondly, and more importantly, Retail Traders have a massive execution advantage. Kenneth Griffin and Douglas Cifu are your friends. Allow me to explain.

For Institutional Traders, the price and quantity they see on the exchange is the price and quantity they get. If a market is 200x15.05 to 100x15.10 and they want to buy 100 shares, 100 shares fill at $15.10 and then the ask evaporates, making it more difficult to buy shares (hence why Institutional Investors gravitate towards large caps with plentiful liquidity).

It’s an entirely different setup for Retail Traders.

A slew of market makers, Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Virtu Financial, gleefully pay your broker for the opportunity to fill your order at a better price at near unlimited quantity, because in general Retail Traders are wrong on a short-term timeframe. In the same market (200x15.05 to 100x15.10) where an Institutional Trader struggles to buy more than 100 shares, you might be able to buy 1,500 or even 3,600 at $15.0879. The market maker is happy to sell at $15.0879 because their model thinks the true price is $15.075, but you got a great deal and were able to execute significantly more efficiently than a larger a Institutional Investor.

What this means is if you cast a wide enough net and wait patiently for attractive entries, you can dance in and out of excellent risk-to-reward setups that are simply off-limits to Institutional Investors due to execution constraints.

I’m changing things up for this article. I’m focusing on four new names I’ve been buying starter positions in this week, and following the “early-stage” format of the 2023 IGI Pitch. Maybe they’ll go on to become larger positions, maybe the stories fall apart and they don’t.

All of them seem to be rapidly inflecting and have significant 2026 tailwinds, yet are priced as if everyone is skeptical, or more likely, unaware of the stories. Of course it’s possible the narratives fizzle out, but at the valuations they are trading at I think they are too compelling to ignore.

The Trades

Trade #1: “The Little Pawn-Shop That Could”

Sector: Consumers

LONG Cash Converters International (CCV:Australia)

200,000 Shares $0.33 AUD

P/E: 9.2x

2026 P/E: 7.6x

Price to Tangible Book: 1.18x

Dividend: 5.88%

Market Cap: 213 Million AUD

Current Price: $0.34 AUD

Short-Term Target: $0.38 AUD

Long-Term Target: $0.45 AUD

Cash Converters International is a rapidly inflecting International pawn shop operator with 659 company-owned and franchised stores across the United Kingdom, Europe, South Africa, Australia, and New Zealand.

From humble beginnings as a single pawn shop in Western Australia in 1984, Cash Converters expanded rapidly via its capital-light franchising model and a focus on financial services. As with all companies, excessive growth comes with bloat and inefficiency and by 2020 Cash Converters’ expansion into payday and vehicle lending was souring.

In 2020, Sam Budiselik, an Investment Banker with experience at Patersons Securities, Barclays, UBS, and Deutsche Bank, was installed as CEO and embarked on three key initiatives: expense control, winding down the volatile payday and vehicle lending segments, and expanding the company’s footprint by buying out Cash Converters franchises at extremely attractive multiples.

His efforts yielded immediate results; in 2021 the company swung from a loss of 2 cents per share to a profit of 3 cents and announced a two cent annual dividend, the first since 2016.

What I like about Cash Converts (aside from the dirt cheap valuation and inflecting story) is its natural growth runway: acquiring franchisees at rock-bottom valuations.

Since 2020, Cash Converters has bought out 79 franchises in Australia and the UK at an average EBITDA multiple under 5x and an IRR upwards of 15%. It purchased 42 stores from Franchise Operator Capital Cash in the UK at 6.3x Pre-Tax Profits in 2022, purchased 10 additional stores from a UK Franchise Partner in July 2025 (with a 12 M Debt Facility from Llyods bank), and just last month concluded the acquisition of 14 Australian franchise stores at just 4.3x EBITDA using cash on hand.

While the stock itself trades at 5x EBITDA, I think the success of the acquisitions at 4-5x EBITDA is indicative of Cash Converter’s growth trajectory. Not only does it have a tailwind from improving credit quality as its loan book stabilizes as payday and vehicle loans roll off, it can continue to allocate its $72 Million AUD cash balance in highly accretive acquisitions that immediately help the bottom line.

It’s also important to note that Cash Converter’s earnings are stronger than they seem. The company amortizes approximately 3.5 Million AUD of intangibles a year, adjusting for this and other adjustments, the company is closer to an 8x multiple.

There’s also a dark horse that I think provides further surprise upside. EZCorp International (EZPW), one of the largest pawn store operators in the US, Mexico, and Central America, owns 43% of Cash Converters (275 Million shares), and has purchased 61 Million on the open market since Sam Budiselik became CEO. I think EZCorp is monitoring the turnaround story, and given their stock trades at 12.5x forward earnings while Cash Converters is trading at just 7.6x, it’s possible they may one day be interested in an all stock acquisition which would be immediately accretive to their bottom line and open the door to Europe and Australia.

Sam Budiselik has already demonstrated the turnaround nature of the company after resuscitating Earnings Per Share from -$0.0374 in 2020 to $0.0369 in 2025 (not to mention doubling the stock price), and his alignment via ownership of 20 Million shares gives me additional confidence the company is on the right track.

Simply put, I think Cash Converters is a growth story trading at an extremely attractive valuation in a counter-cyclical industry, likely due to its small size and total lack of institutional ownership. It’s investor friendly (the CEO makes a strong case for owning the stock), primed for significant growth in 2026, and has all the markings of a company that would become a beloved “Fintwit Compounder”, if it was 10x the size and people knew about it.

The CEO has also indicated the stock will join the ASX All Ordinaries Index in just a few weeks, which I think adds an event-driven element to this trade.

The stock has been moving as the good earnings and acquisition news continues to roll in, but given the alignment and growth potential I think it’s certainly attractive at 7.6x forward earnings and I plan to add heavily at the $0.30 AUD - $0.32 AUD range should it head lower.

Trade #2: "Slow and Steady, then All at Once"

Sector: Technology

LONG Software Research Associates (3817:Tokyo)

5,400 Shares ¥ 4,680

P/E: 13.4x

2026 P/E: 12.6x

Dividend: 3.68%

Market Cap: ¥ 74 Billion ($500 Million USD)

Current Price: ¥ 4,890

Short-Term Target: ¥ 5,100

Long-Term Target: ¥ 5,500

SRA Holdings is a Japanese holding company specializing in outsourced software development in the healthcare, educational, and financial industries and the distribution of cloud solutions and consultancy via its AIT (Advanced Integration Tech) subsidiary.

Founded in 1967 as Software Research Associates, SRA has grown significantly over the past 20 years via highly beneficial partnerships. It’s Advanced Integration Tech subsidiary was originally a joint venture with IBM, and they remain closely aligned as AIT is one of the most well-known consultants for migration to IBM’s Cloud and is also a leading distributor of custom IBM software such as IBM SPSS within the Japanese banking and life insurance industries. In 2017, SRA acquired Cavirin Systems, a developer of cloud vulnerability detection software, and in 2018, acquired Proxim Wireless, as US developer of 5G wireless connectivity solutions. In 2024, SRA sold a minority stake in its OSS (Open Source Software) Subsidiary to NTT Data to further their collaboration and development of data storage technology.

What I like about SRA is its cross-selling potential. Not only does SRA develop niche, sticky software for clients such as “UniVision” for Universities (handles campus administration, registration, reservations, financial funds disbursement, etc) and “Healthplayer” for hospitals (medical charts, record delivery, etc) that generate substantial annual recurring revenue, SRA has a further opportunity to generate sizeable consulting fees from the management of its client’s data storage and cloud server appetite. This has enabled SRA to “lock down” customers and in turn steadily fatten its profit margins, by slowly hiking prices for its software and consultancy offerings.

Revenue has grown by about 8% a year since 2021 and recent August guidance has affirmed a 2026 target for an additional 6.5% in revenue and earnings growth. While SRA operates at a significantly lower operating margin relative to pure-play Saas names such as Pro-Ship 3763 (30% margin), I think the unique combination of SRA’s high margin software development unit and lower margin IT management and consultancy services has allowed SRA to develop an extremely sticky customer base that is difficult to disrupt. If anyone is to benefit from AI reducing software development costs, it’s probably SRA given the fact many clients have outsoured their entire software and IT stack to SRA, and SRA will directly benefit from higher productivity.

SRA has quietly played the long game, bringing in new clients, steadily increasing prices at reasonable levels (not FICO), and earnings and the stock slowly marched towards fresh highs.

Recent Q1 2025 earnings were meddled by an FX and impairment charge, and while the 12.6x Forward P/E isn’t dirt cheap like some of the other Japanese names I own like 9478, I think there is more than meets the eye here.

SRA Holdings is debt free, and in typical Japanese fashion has a massive Securities Portfolio of 9.323 Billion Yen. Little is known about the Securities Portfolio other than it has unrealized gains of 5.876 Billion Yen and that 7% of the portfolio is invested in Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group. If you add up that to the 18.99 Billion Yen in cash SRA has, there is approximately ¥ 2,373 in cash and securities per share.

This flies under the radar as Bloomberg doesn’t count securities as cash in net debt calculations, but what this really means is (or at least how I think of it) is that of the ¥ 4,885 share price, you are paying just ¥ 2,512 for the software business itself since ¥ 2,373 is already cash and equities, which matches index performance anyways. It’s like buying a software business and getting bank and brokerage accounts included in the price.

While SRA isn’t necessarily as exciting of a name as Cash Converters, I think its unique approach and steady, predictable growth make it too cheap to ignore at 12x 2026 earnings. The dividend has steadily increased from just ¥ 70 a decade ago to ¥ 180 today (a yield of 3.68%), and given the borrow cost in Japan is just 1.34%, the cost of “financing” a position like this rather than converting your dollars is entirely covered by the dividend.

The company has decent insider ownership of around 10% and interestingly boasts Hikari Tsushin as a 2.25% holder in addition to some value funds such as Polar Capital and Samarang Deep Value.

I think the ¥ 4,800 - ¥ 5,050 range is attractive, and I plan on adding heavily if we drop to ¥ 4,600 as that represents 11.5x 2026 earnings. SRA’s recent monthly report last night indicated a drop in August AIT bookings, but I am not too concerned since they are up 31% YTD and these bookings are historically very variable. While SRA isn’t a “get rich quick” name with an imminent event-driven catalyst people are so chasing, it’s a quiet outperformer that I think is worth your attention.

Trade #3: "Front Running the Dividend Guys"

Sector: Banking

LONG Mechanics Bancorp (MCHB:Nasdaq)

6,000 Shares $12.90

2026 P/E: 10.6x

Estimated 2026 Dividend: 8.5%

Market Cap: $2.3 Billion USD

Current Price: $12.90

Short-Term Target: $13.50

Long-Term Target: $15.00

Does this chart look familiar? It should ring a bell.

If you recognize it immediately, points to you. Mechanics Bancorp is the product of the merger between Homestreet (HMST:Nasdaq) and Mechanics Bancorp (MCHB:OTC). While the new combined entity has the stock ticker history of Homestreet, the vast majority of assets (74%) were contributed by Mechanics, and their shareholders own 91.7% of the combination; you should consider it an entirely new entity.

Mechanics is a straightforward story, it’s a well-run bank with significant alignment, and is set to become a cash cow. Nearly 77% of the newly restructured company is owned by the Ford Financial Fund, a private equity operator with a history of success in banking. Mechanics was already an outperformer and synergies set to be realized by the middle of 2026 should propel earnings to a record high of $302 Million, which would imply the stock is trading at under 10x 2026 EPS.

The stock trades at a relatively expensive 1.7x Price to Tangible Book, but there’s good reason why. Not only does Mechanics generate a top ROE, it’s largest dividend target is a rarity in banking. The private equity owners of Mechanics are ready to finally see a payout, and they intend achieve this by running the bank with a massive payout ratio upwards of 90%.

Given the bank’s own 2026 EPS target of $1.31, a payout ratio of 90% would imply a dividend yield of 9.2%, and even if you knock earnings down to $1.20 the implied dividend yield is still an impressive 8.3%.

What I like about the Mechanic’s setup is you don’t have to worry about capital management. The Ford Financial Fund isn’t interested in pursuing reckless growth or wild acquisitions, they own 75% and want the bank to be run conservatively return profits. They also may one day be interested in a sale.

Mechanic’s is a special situation. Due to some confusion about its history and near-term lack of equity research coverage, I think most are still unaware of the comeback aspect.

Mechanic’s has two relatively near-term tailwinds, index reconstitution and the dividend policy.

The merger with Homestreet closed last Monday, and the combined market cap has increased significantly. I’m not an expert on index reconstitution and the free float methodology used, but it stands to reason that even if Mechanics does not qualify for an intra-quarter special Russell Rebalance as a result of the merger, its weight will significantly increase next June leading to increased passive ownership.

Additionally, if there’s one powerful investing bloc who’s willing to look past almost anything, it’s the dividend junkies. Like a man madly in love with a New York socialite wildly out of his league who occasionally texts him at 3 AM for tax assistance, the dividend investors are in general willing to overlook almost any red flag in pursuit of flashy yield. The proof is in BDC’s and MREITs. Industry losers such as BCP Investment Corp, Armour Residential REIT, and Prospect Capital Corp have routinely generated subpar returns (worse than savings accounts) while issuing additional equity constantly, and yet their investor base is always willing to smile and forgive.

Why? The dividend, of course! Slap a 7 or 8% yield on something and all is well. “The dividend speaks for itself” they’ll tell you. It’s the same setup as the ETF structured product lovers who love a 10% “dividend” even though most of it is a return of capital.

Mechanics is a totally different trade. It’s dividend will be funded by strong earnings, and as earnings and the dividend increase, Mechanics will become a unique diamond in the rough: one of the only banks paying out 90%+ of earnings at an 8%+ yield. By that point I suspect the cat will be out of the bag, the dividend investors will be foaming at the mouth and Mechanics may trade at a much more premium 11-12x earnings as a result of dividend investor interest.

All of mechanics peers trade in the 11x-21x range, which makes the setup even more peculiar given Mechanic’s sizeable dividend target and it’s peer-leading Return on Tangible Equity.

I think the risk-to-reward is attractive enough here at $12.90 for a starter position and becomes even more attractive in the lower 12s, where I suspect a lot of bargain hunters are waiting for. Absent a blowup in California CRE or some type of hidden credit issues in Homestreet’s portfolio that Mechanic’s didn’t sniff out, I think you are looking at downside of perhaps $11 to $12 a share if the name is not well received as attention builds, and upside towards $14 to $15 a share by next year as increased passive ownership and the dividend builds.

Trade #4: "Full Dividend Junkie"

Sector: Banking

LONG Merchant’s Bancorp 7.625% Series E Preferred (MBINL)

1,200 Shares $23.21

Current Yield: 8.1%

Strip Yield: 8.3%

Qualified Dividend Treatment (Lower Tax Rate): Yes

Merchant’s Bancorp preferred stock has fallen significantly this year as a result of mortgage fraud issues encountered in the second quarter. Despite a massive $43 Million provision for fraudulent loans, Merchant’s Bank was still profitable and earned 60 cents a share.

Understandably, the fixed income guys were shaken up by the mortgage fraud provisions and a sharp selloff in the bank’s preferred stock ensued. Significant panic selling occurred in the Series E Preferred just a few weeks ago.

Merchant’s Bancorp Preferred Series E, MBINL currently trades at $23.40 for a current yield of 8.1% and a strip yield of 8.3%, which I find attractive. Merchant’s Bancorp itself is a beneficiary of lower rates given their current credit issues and high exposure to commercial real estate. Additionally, Merchant’s has a sizeable residential mortgage arm that is poised to benefit from increased activity if mortgage rates decline.

Ultimately, I think Merchant’s Bancorp will work their way through the troubled loans. CEO Michael F Petrie Owns 12 Million shares (384 Million, 27% of the company), and assorted insiders own a further 4 Million shares. The bank is sitting on Tier 1 Capital of $2.1 Billion, and I think they have ample capacity to absorb further loan losses should they arise.

With MBINL, you are getting paid a “reputational premium”.

I think nearly everyone believes the company is OK and will work through its issues even if they need to take a further $50 - $75 Million loan loss provision, but Institutional Investors on the credit side are hesitant to own the preferreds as it looks extremely bad if the name blows up and they go to zero. I think this outcome is unlikely.

Merchant’s Bancorp Series D MBINM (with an 8.25% coupon) is currently trading above par at $25.245, so I think the opportunity in MBINL is largely exists because a sizeable holder got cold feet and blew out of the name in early August, and the price hasn’t recovered.

As with any name with active regulatory or credit issues, I think it makes sense to size this trade extremely small. Unlike pure equities investing where diversification past a certain point doesn’t actually reduce risk, diversification in preferred investing certainly does. I wouldn’t pay anything more than $23.65, as I don’t think a strip yield below 8.2% is worth it.

Preferred ETFs are inflecting as people begin to chase yield again, and at 8.30% I think MBINL presents a nice opportunity to sprinkle yield into your portfolio as long as you size it small.

Final Thoughts

Of the four trades, I like Cash Converters the most as I think the story is powerful and easy to understand. They make an excellent case on why they are a significantly different company than they were just a few years ago, and it seems like a name that has entirely flown off the radar despite it’s continual announcement of good news. I think attractive risk to reward is present in the other three trades as well, and while you aren’t going to get an Oracle level return I think they provide an excellent way to get exposure to “value” at attractive multiples.

As with any trade, and especially with these turnarounds and special situations in formative stages, I think it makes sense to start small and see how the stories evolve.
